Most people wildly lowball what a data breach really costs. They picture the ransom and stop right there. But the ransom is usually the smallest piece of it. Downtime alone can dwarf whatever you handed the attacker. Then the legal bills and the fines come. Lost customers and months of cleanup show up long after.

Waiting around for flawless risk data is how these projects die a slow death. There is never enough clean history to feel sure. So teams keep polishing and never present anything. Meanwhile, the budget cycle sails past, and nothing gets funded. A rough, honest estimate today beats a perfect one that turns up after the decision is already made.

The ranking comes from one calculation per candidate control. Expected loss before, minus expected loss after, divided by cost. Order the list by that ratio and the budget builds itself, including the part that says stop.

Measures reducing how often an event occurs, covering access restriction, patching cadence and phishing resistance. They lower the number of draws and leave the severity of any event that still happens unchanged.
Expected loss after the control is in place, assessed individually rather than as a bundle.

Nothing after the first step works without the first step. An organization with no current exposure figure in September cannot produce a ranked list by November, which makes baselining the task to start before budget season rather than during it.

An exposure figure from before the spend and one from after, produced by the same method with the differences between them attributable to specific changes. A figure recalculated on a revised model proves nothing about the controls.
